title: When AI Takes Notes: Court Allows Privacy Claims Against Otter.ai to Proceed

reading.body:
A speech-to-text system is alleged to have recorded workplace meetings by default without obtaining consent from all participants, then used those recordings to train its AI model. The system was integrated into widely-used video conferencing platforms and could join meetings automatically through calendar integrations, making its recording activity potentially invisible to users. It is not established whether the recordings were actually used for training, whether anonymization occurred, or what the legal outcome will be.

The failure is a deployment without adequate consent mechanisms and without making users aware of the system's recording and data use practices. Users who did not install or configure the system themselves could be recorded without their knowledge. Catching this would have required explicit opt-in for recording before joining any meeting, clear notification to all participants that recording was active, and transparent explanation of how recordings would be used.

What is not established: whether Otter.ai violated applicable law, whether the privacy policy disclosures were legally sufficient, or the factual details of the incidents alleged in the lawsuit.

summary:
# Summary

A federal lawsuit filed in California accuses Otter.ai, a popular speech-to-text transcription service, of secretly recording private work conversations without proper consent and using them to train its artificial intelligence systems. The suit, brought by Justin Brewer from San Jacinto, alleges that Otter's transcription tool, which works with Zoom, Google Meet, and Microsoft Teams, records meetings by default without asking all participants for permission. The company claims it has about 25 million users and has processed over 1 billion meetings since its 2016 founding.

The lawsuit argues that while Otter's privacy policy mentions data training in fine print, many users remain unaware their conversations are being shared with the company and third parties. The complaint challenges Otter's claim that it anonymizes audio before using it for machine learning, stating the company provides no public explanation of how it removes confidential information. Recent complaints on social media have highlighted instances where Otter automatically joined meetings through integrated workplace calendars and recorded sensitive business discussions, including one case where confidential details were shared with unintended recipients.
